title: Some thoughts about black comedy and changing cultural attitudes after watching M*A*S*H for the first time last night

commenti.body: The misogyny in that movie is real tough. The way they treat “hot lips” did not feel like a joke at all and it definitely hurt the movie for me. I honestly felt bad for the actress and it’s for sure an reflection of the times.

I think this analysis is fair. I watched MASH for the first time as a teenager and that was a time I was more available to laugh at bullying. The show is kinder even as it draws laughs from dark places.

I’m a huge Altman fan though, and I suggest you check out more of his movies. There are lots of great ones, including McCabe & Mrs. Miller, Nashville, The Player, Gosford Park, and more.

I haven't seen it in decades, but I remember being a little underwhelmed. But I'm much more knowledgeable about politics, so this is one of those rare films I'd consider giving a second chance. My mother lived through the Korean war and met my white dad in peace time. The Korean war had hawks who believed the atom bomb would've won the war and in retrospect saved more lives. My grandparents were in Japan during the firebombing, so that informs my perception about the wars in East Asia. However, the racist internment of Japanese Americans, Eisenhower's belief using the bomb was unnecessary, and the fact that the Soviets invaded soon after the bomb makes the use of the bomb more suspect. 

The person who leaked the Pentagon papers said on the docunentary Hearts and Minds, "We weren't on the wrong side. We were the wrong side." I don't see what, besides retrospect, makes the war in Vietnam less justifiable than the Korean War. Had Nixon not "thrown a monkey wrench" on the peace process for his political future, perhaps we'd have a democratic Vietnam or South Vietnam. Altman made the film when the Vietnam War was facing plenty of backlash and was in the forefront of the minds of the audience. My favorite Altman film is Secret Honor, a one man show of Nixon having a meltdown when dictatong his autobiography. It also has dark humor. 

One comedian said of comedy isn't able to lift our spirits when we feel the worse, what use is it? That's not to say comedy is never cruel or ugly. Many comedians note how so much comedy ages like milk. The knowing laugh aspect of Todd Solondz is one of the main reasons why he'd be the best director to adapt my life into a movie (I know that would never happen). John Waters satirized Sirk in polyester. He thought if satire isn't made out of love for what's being satirized, it won't be as good.
[removed]

MASH was a little movie by a little known TV director that was a surprise hit at the time and gave that director the boost needed to forge a career as a filmmaker. It took the wind out of the sails of the other big war comedy from that year, *Catch 22*. 

I'm sure that part of why it was popular was *because* the humor was so ribald and sexist. It was daring and dark and the kind of comedy you couldn't get on television. Few movies before dared to be so light-hearted while drenched in the blood of war. Dr. Strangelove was a great war satire, but the violence of war is kept off screen. The 1965 movie *King Rat* might be in similar territory, but I think that was when the horror of Vietnam was just starting to become real for American audiences. *Catch 22* also combines gore and comedy, but still keeps the horror and humor separate.

Roger Ebert called MASH "Sgt. Bilko for adults" and does a [great job explaining why it's funny](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/mash-1970). At the time the gore was the more unsettling aspect of the film, not the sexism. Today we're more desensitized to the gore of war and don't react to it the same way.

Of course, it led to one of the best TV sitcoms of all time where they toned down all the roughest parts of the film and found a way to make it all palatable.

It's pre-second wave feminism. Much of postwar culture, even when anti-establishment in tone, is blithely sexist by today's standards.

And to be honest with you, there wasn't much difference between the attitudes in MASH and those when I was growing up in the nineties, but you'd be less likely to find them in the ostensibly "progressive" or radical post second-wave.

He doesn’t really explain why it is funny, he is operating from the position that it is funny and then is justifying it. I did not find the sadism amusing or relatable at all, whereas he did.

“We laugh, not because "MASH" is Sgt. Bilko for adults, but because it is so true to the unadmitted sadist in all of us.”

That's what I'm saying - it was a different time and audiences then found it funny. It struck a nerve, which is why comedy is one of the most elusive genres. It reflects that attitudes of the times and doesn't always stand the test of time. There's no reason why it needs to.

I'm guessing the Vietnam War and the specter of nuclear war created so much national tension that a movie like MASH comes along and relieves that tension. If you aren't living in those times it's harder to see the humor. But I also think that having it come out of nowhere was part of it, kind of like *Easy Rider* - which is also not the most fantastic movie but it struck a nerve with audiences at the time.

MASH wasn't my generation. I first watched MASH in the early 80s after I was already very familiar with the TV show, and just thought "well, the TV show was a lot better." But even in the 80s that kind of misogyny was pretty commonplace and not shocking. MASH was just a little more extreme about it.

Sure, that is fair. I guess I was hoping to find a way in, but you have made a very strong case for why I should probably accept that it is a dated object to be appreciated more from a historical perspective than actively enjoyed.

The good thing is that Altman has made many many much better films.

I think *Nashville* is also dated (but much easier to appreciate) but most of his movies hold up and a few are due for rediscovery (like *Images*).

I admire Altman and still love *Nashville*, *The player*, *Gosford Park*... but had the same reaction to MASH recently, so much so that I got rid of it (unusual for me, you'd think I'm curating stuff for The Museum Of My Life, the way I cling to it).

The breezy anti-authoritarianism is, as I recall, the most appealing thing about it all, BUT, in retrospect, it's packaged with such a dose of White Man Can Do Anything To Anyone, it's simply unpleasant. Just imagine two black guys behaving like those two. Even less point mentioning women, short of porn it's hard to think of a movie in which they are more clearly things.

So I get how it once seemed fresh and liberating, but it just isn't. It's great for white men Main Characters. Nobody else need apply.

> The 1965 movie King Rat 

great book

It's also possible that the sexism was criticized when it came out and Altman took note and treated female characters better after that. Maybe we wouldn't have gotten *Three Women* otherwise. He found a muse in Shelley Duvall.
Cool, this is encouraging and has me excited to dig into his filmography more.

Over and above the comments on the casual sexism made here, which I agree with completely, there's the question of whether it is in fact funny in any other way.

The cross-talking in surgery is fun for a little while but grates badly after a few scenes.

The climactic scene where they take "Painless" to a joke suicide last supper is excruciatingly awful, about as funny as a cold bag of sick.

I remember watching it back around 1978 (school film club) and thinking it was pretty awful then. The comparison with Catch-22 didn't go well for this film even then, and that's with all the evident flaws of Catch-22.
Nah, you just got a bad sense of humor. MASH absolutely holds up.

I havent watched MASH, but I very much agree with the shift in the zeitgeist.


My main frame would be a shift from nietzschean master towards slave morality.

Basically the exploding capitalism of the post war period created this athmosphere of all pervasive chauvinism or machismo, interestingly all the way down to the lowest strata of society, and also from the left into the right.


If you look at the post 70s leftism it has that same vibe of aloof superiority of the self-actualized educated academics towards the simple minded proles. And then the proles do not espouse christian humility and solidarity either but just counter with their own version of their superiority complex. Everybody vs. everybody.


But as long as the ponzi scheme of expanding capital went on that all worked out somehow. Now with the millenials onwards the ponzi scheme explodes, the limits are made clear by climate change, we have in large swathes been utterly humbled and are now desperately trying to shift towards a new mode of slave morality.


The main cultural product to point to would be Judd Apatow movies imho. The thing is that we are now all the loser nerds and not the big dick machos, how even the majority might have felt in previous generations. Even if someone is moderately successful they can still see that everybody continuing to just lick their teeth will just lead us all into hell.

I wonder how much of the change in reception has to do with most current audiences having no frame of reference for the terror many young men must have been feeling with the draft in place at that time. Just an assumption on my part, but I imagine there must have been a rage towards military authority on a much greater scale than we’ve seen since then.

Not trying to excuse the sexism however. It’s bad.

MASH is from a different era, where what was funny was different than today.       
Beyond that, it is a very cynical film. The characters are not super nice guys by any means. That is intentional. It fits with the military humor, people being assholes and amoral is part of the culture. A lot of military humor is in 'poor taste' at the best of times.      

MASH is basically what you get when you write a story about a bunch of jocks thrown into a military drama who go around flipping tables and telling the heroes that they're a bunch of putzes.      
Those 'jocks' were what men in that era imagined themselves as being. Freewheeling renegades that did what they wanted with a grin on their face and a woman on their arm.      
These days, the equivalent would be a genre savvy quippy action hero who shook up the place and stood up for the little guys (and gals) because his heart was so big. That or a girl boss that came in and humiliated all the stodgy conservatives and ran the entire camp better than they ever could.

My impression for the casual *crude* sexism of that time is that what it wasn't is it wasn't the 'chivalrous' sexism of what came before and was therefore anti-authoritarian.  It also stripped off any pretext, providing a clearer target.  In its own way, it served some kind of good by removing the fig leaf, although that was unlikely the intent.  The intent was to shock the powers that be.
I think this is a productive line of thought, because I did clock that Hawkeye was explicitly mentioned to be a draftee.
You say that, but Shakespeare is much older and still funny. MASH was criticized in its time for its unabashed hatred of women. Eventually that lead to the far superior latter half of the Tv show.

I believe that when approaching old movies, you have to take into account the times they were made in.  In M\*A\*S\*H's case counterculture, the recent end of the Vietnam war, anti-authoritarian, and there are some great discussions/comments below.
Couldn't agree more.

Shakespeare was misogynistic too. Ever read The Taming of the Shrew?      
If misogyny is going to turn you off of humor, your trip through comedy in film is going to end some time about 2010.

This. I sort of get annoyed how people view everything from a modern cultural lens now. My parents both love MASH - my dad’s a Nam Vet and my mom was a hippie and feminist and they both love it. 

Maybe it’s hard for people now to empathize with the culture of those who this movie was contemporary for because there’s so much negativity against boomers. I’m weird in that most people my age don’t have parents as old as mine, so I’ve been privy to a slightly different perspective than my peers.

I think what the OP is avoiding is the film's clear narrative context: war. It's not like the film is set in a hospital in Miami or something. I know it's hard to imagine, but war is even worse than casual racism or sexism. In fact, it's much worse. For inducing sheer human misery, nothing beats war.

M\*A\*S\*H was incredibly popular at the time, because it didn't hold back its contempt for obedient, authoritarian military figures (especially by-the-book characters like Hot Lips and the Robert Duvall character). Sure, Sutherland and Gould weaponize sexism and cruel pranks to inflict pain on their military targets (and, yes, it was somewhat morally questionable even in 1970), but the general public (especially young, draft-aged men) really got a kick out of watching stiff, bloviating war hawks suffer indignity. 

I'm not sure how to create a modern-day equivalent of M\*A\*S\*H. Maybe imagine a media personality who is obnoxious and irritating (for me it would be Piers Morgan); and now imagine that person taking the piss out of a far, far worse mass-murdering monster (e.g. Putin). 

"Not the hero we asked for..."

It’s one of my favourites. And a lot of the humour in that play continues to be funny, if only because it’s tweaked in presentation for the modern day. 

My point is not that Shakespeare had no sexism in it, but rather than his plays still being funny is evidence that comedy “aging like milk” isn’t inevitable like some say it is. Shakespeare still being funny for many of its jokes shows there’s universal themes and concepts that remain humourous.
I mean…Shylock has aged pretty roughly
…okay? What does that have to do with what we’re discussing?
I just found your assertion that shakespeare’s comedy has aged well to be a little reductive. A lot of it has been sanitized for modern sensibilities.

I should’ve made my point clearer. I don’t mean every single line in every single play has remained relevant, tasteful, and interesting to every single human being in every generation that ever lived. I mean that the fact people still laugh when watching Shakespeare plays at many of the jokes proves that humour isn’t destined to be unfunny after time passes. I still find things in Norse and Greek mythology funny that were intended to be funny, and those are thousands of years old. Some comedy can last. Comedy isn’t destined to die and become irrelevant. That doesn’t mean all of Shakespeare is unimpeachable. 

Shylock even has some funny lines that still land, even if the character himself is seen as a caricature these days. He wasn’t really intended to be a pure comical character, though, so he feels irrelevant to the discussion. I will say ‘Shylock’ is an Interesting accompanying piece. 

I shouldn’t have mentioned Mash’s misogyny so soon after that remake, but contextualized it. There is NOTHING in the film that is still funny, not one thing, and people saying ‘it wasn’t misogynist back then, it was normal and super funny’ are wrong - it was highly criticized and lots of people didn’t find it funny. Meanwhile, the latter season of the TV show still hold up decades later. When Margaret is a proper character and the ‘sexual assault as humour’ is pulled back for more universally funny jokes that DO still hold up.
That’s so funny, I think mash the movie is still funny as hell! Love the show too

Then it’s lasted. Personally I can’t quite find misogyny of that degree funny, but there will always be be someone who does (not saying that’s why you find it funny, but many people do like to see women degraded and that’s a constant as some humour). Many things, good and bad, can last the ages.
Obviously I don’t find the misogyny funny
But that is 85% of the jokes.

That’s absolutely not true. There’s one particularly harrowing sequence with Margaret that is rough to watch, but most of the movie’s humor is derived from the nihilistic casual attitute the surgeons have in the face of a deeply brutal war they want no part in. I definitely understand why the rough misogyny in the movie would stick out as longer in the runtime, but it’s just not true

The recent end of the Vietnam War? Altman's movie was released in 1970, while the war was still raging and killing thousands. The end of the Vietnam War was still five years away.

Boys in the audience could realistically look forward to being drafted and possibly reduced to bleeding, jagged flesh on the operating table as in M\*A\*S\*H or even coming home in a box.

The terror was very real. Even the men who came home alive were frequently traumatized in body and/or mind.

That’s an ongoing theme and something for the occasional jab, but the bulk of the escapades have them creeping on women or forcing themselves on them, and we’re meant to find these ‘pranks’ the high points of hilarity.

It's probably fair to note that before it was a film, it was a novel written by an Army doctor under a pen name and it came out in 1968, right at the height of the Vietnam war protests and the beginning of the Nixon administration. The success of the novel is what led to the adaptation, and its anti-war stance is clearly informed by that latter conflict and by the growing distaste at the time for the horrors of armed conflict. 

There was quite a lot of frat-boy grossness in the novel as well, but what remains is nevertheless toned down a bit for the film. But sexual stereotypes from the '50s, filtered through the combined fields of both medicine and war (neither endeavor lacking of misogyny) adapted in 1970 and viewed through a modern lens are not gonna hold up very well.  They don't mistreat Houlihan simply because she's a woman. They mistreat her because they're doctors and she's a nurse. It wasn't right but it certainly was the way of the world those folks had grown up in.

I agree with you, OP - the sense of humour in MASH is dated. It feels blokeish and mean-spirited at times. But Altman made a ton of great films, so I'd urge you to check some of them out. My favourites, apart from The Long Goodbye (which is probably my overall favourite) are:

\- 3 Women

\- McCabe & Mrs. Miller

\- Nashville

\- Thieves Like Us

\- The Player

\- Gosford Park 

\- Secret Honor (strictly speaking a made-for-TV movie)

\- Short Cuts

It’s also right place right time criticism of Vietnam replicated beautifully with an entire full set. It’s covered by “Korea” but it’s Vietnam and people at the time needed a laugh from such dark and depressing subject matters. Altman balances a beautiful line of comedy and serious with this film. the tent chock full of injured soldiers when Duke and Hawkeye beg for a chest cutter ,how bloody and gory the operating table scenes are.

These guys were putting soldiers together like meatballs because they had to use whatever was available to them. It’s a big product of its time and military culture was like that with the sexism, the drinking, the trouble making. Introducing Mash units to war amputations rates from WW2 to the Korean War dropped from 36% to 13%. A seriously wounded soldier if he made it to a MASH unit during the Korean War had a 97% chance of survival. These guys were great doctors and were giving up lucrative careers to patch up kids thousands of miles away from home.

Altman really made an incredibly unique anti war comedy in a time when no one dared touch the subject in that way.

If you had been in the military in the 1950s you think you’d be any different as any of the males ? I don’t think you understand how crazy and reckless the military has been especially during wartime in the past and especially with the “boys will be boys attitude.”

Yes, I feel that today's audiences are completely desensitized to the war aspect of MASH. We've been so inundated by gore and violence that it means nothing. Instead people are disturbed by the one thing you don't see in today's films and that's the rampant sexism. Times have changed.
I’m not going to ask you to watch the movie again because clearly you don’t like it, but you’re pretty blatantly wrong, so I don’t really know what else to say
Maybe I’ll rewatch it, then. I saw it in high school and almost threw the TV out the window I was so disgusted, but I’ve enjoyed Seasons 4-9 of the TV show since then.

> Nah, you just got a bad sense of humor. MASH absolutely holds up.

What I think u/TheZoneHereros is talking about is best exemplified by the scene where they expose Hot Lips, naked, to the camp. Which is cruel, isn't funny, or at least doesn't translate to modern sensibilities. They are bullying her and in modern films (or even older films like Carrie, four years later, where the pig blood dump is a similar scene) the bullies are the bad guys. And then bullying Frank Burns so much that he's carted off in a straitjacket. And bullying the nurses in Tokyo. None of those things are funny, but aside from funny, we just have such a different viewpoint on bullying these days. 

u/death_by_chocolate writes:

> They don't mistreat Houlihan simply because she's a woman. They mistreat her because they're doctors and she's a nurse. It wasn't right but it certainly was the way of the world those folks had grown up in.

Which is true, but the film presents that as comic relief, not as critical of it, or even having taken a step back from it. The part about homosexuality is a bit weird as well, not so much with the homosexuality, but in how they choose to try to resolve the "problem" in a very creepy way (that Spike Lee tried to borrow from 15 years later and was criticized harshly for, especially by Roger Ebert). MASH was ahead of its time in other ways, it knows how to present racism "correctly" and how to present the horrors of war in a new and newly "correct" way, which is part of its power and popularity. And innovation. The sexual content, however, like the shower scene, is presented as entertainment for the audience, vicariously, our POV is that of the doctors, their enjoyment is ours. Which still works for 95% of the film, it just can trigger us (for lack of a better word) today in this one category.

Well said. That exact scene would be played for horror in modern movies (if you've seen Birds of Prey, the Harley Quinn movie, there is a scene of a woman being forced to strip or dance that was very disturbing, for instance), and when the cinematic language and tropes have changed so much, it makes for very strange viewing. Some of the scenes that were intended to be comic relief feel so mean spirited that they are actually tense and hard to get through, and the effect is that the pacing and tone of the movie get thrown off wildly and the viewing experience is not very good.

Did you read how Roger Ebert explains that scene? 

> When they are matter-of-factly cruel to "Hot Lips" Hoolihan, we cannot quite separate that from the matter-of-fact way they've got to put wounded bodies back together again. "Hot Lips," who is all Army professionalism and objectivity, is less human because the suffering doesn't reach her.
>
>I think perhaps that's what the movie is about. Gould and Sutherland and the members of their merry band of pranksters are offended because the Army regulars don't feel deeply enough. "Hot Lips" is concerned with protocol, but not with war. And so the surgeons, dancing on the brink of crack-ups, dedicate themselves to making her feel something. Her façade offends them; no one could be unaffected by the work of this hospital, but she is. 

I don't think this negates any criticism, but it does contextualize that scene and gives it meaning that I don't know if most people are thinking of. Think of the arguments they have with her leading up to that scene.

Yeah, it's an interesting collision of two competing power imbalances - authority vs the subjugated, and then male vs female. What she is representing in your mind as you view the scene makes all the difference in how it plays for you. I certainly have gotten some intellectual stimulation from considering what the movie is doing, and my respect for it has grown since reading the responses I've got to this post, but it doesn't change the fact that I expect I will never want to watch it again (especially with so many Altman's I've yet to see) and would recommend others approach it with caution unless they are ready to try to do the work of contextualizing it.

MASH came out on VHS in the early 1980s and we watched it many times. That scene always bothered me, even as an early teen, even back in those days. I couldn't explain it, it was purely visceral. I did *not* have the same reaction to other things in the same time period as I was watching (early 1980s) that were pretty bad, but played for laughs. Sexual assault in Sixteen Candles, Revenge of the Nerds, Carbon Copy. Friends moms would lecture us on the unnecessary exploitation of scenes like the showering in Stripes, but those were obvious--like the scene in MASH. For the SA scenes, you needed to actually think about it a little.

> If Altman was trying to show that war can turn people into pieces of shit

Well, maybe he was and maybe he wasn't.  Too literal or perhaps not literal enough.  Compare your opinion of what happens in MASH to your opinion of what happens in Brewster McCloud.

You are comparing films written  for the underdogs to  feel  better or find self-insert  catharsis, to a film written for the 'cool guys'. The frat boys, the party boys, the guys that won.         
Chasing a  naked girl around and showing her off to  the camp is funny. It is mean, but it is funny. Just like tricking the class nerd or dorky coworker to sing  at  a talent show or karaoke is funny. Or making fun  of the teacher and disrupting the entire class is funny. Talking about how big of a virgin another guy is, is funny. If you are on top, it is hilarious. 

This is what I meant by a sense of humor. You don't have a sense of humor, except when it is set  up in a  'punching up' way. Where the Wimp makes the King of the School  look dumb or silly.       
M*A*S*H is written  for a  different crowd  than you. Being a jock was aspirational. Coming in and knocking over all the dumb stodgy  mooks who think they're  'professionals' and 'serious' was a dream. 

Just being a jock doesn't mean that you're racist. Because a Black dude can party and bring around the girls just as much as a White one.
My bad, I thought it was late 70s, or was that the TV Show?

Have you seen Altman’s own Nashville? There’s a scene where a character who’s expecting to sing ends up having to strip, and it’s played for discomfort. I think Houlighan’s thing is played for comedy, then discomfort, then comedy again

The shower scene is different in the novel.  In the novel the nurses are going to the shower and one of Hawkeye's buddies is catcalling them and referring to them as elephants.  Being negative and insulting.  Then Houlihan goes to Henry Blake and threatens to resign her commission with the same result.  At that point Houlihan more or less disappears, doesn't date Duke and isn't at the football game.  Which is not unusual because the novel is episodic like the movie is.

The Painless episode is different too, no Lt. Dish, he is lowered from a helicopter and dropped to the ground.

I would guess that Ring Lardner Jr. and Altman wanted to have more scenes involving women and to raunch it up a bit, so they made those changes.

The nurses overall are not much of a factor in the novel.  It seems mostly it's a boy's club and women are not allowed.  Hawkeye had his buddies and people he disliked.  But women were not buddies.  I kind of suspect the author minimized the nurses because he and his buddies had families at home and fooling around with the nurses was more of a threat to the families than going to some local Korean girl or a prostitute.  So the prostitute material made the novel and the nurses were excised.
